passage: I am Divyansh, and for most of my second year I texted my mentor Mohit sir before every decision: which elective, which internship form, even which font for my poster. He always answered, and I thought that meant I was being careful. Then he went away for a week to a conference and did not reply. I sat with three options for my project topic and felt strangely stuck, as if I had forgotten how to walk. On the fourth day I wrote a page of my own reasons for each option. When he came back I did not ask what I should do. I said, "This is what I picked and why. What am I missing?" He read it and smiled. "Now we can talk."

qa.q: How long was Mohit away at the conference?
qa.a: He was away for a week.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh feel stuck when Mohit did not reply?
qa.a: He had been checking every decision with Mohit, so he had little practice choosing for himself.

qa.q: What did Divyansh change in how he asked Mohit for advice?
qa.a: He brought his own choice and reasons and asked what he was missing, instead of asking what to do.

qa.q: How might Mohit see the earlier stream of texts?
qa.a: Mohit answered every time, but his smile at the page of reasons suggests he prefers a mentee who thinks first. 🙂

grounding: A student who waits for a mentor's instructions brings his own reasoning and grows toward independent judgement.

passage:
At the civil engineering firm in Chennai, Uday had a habit: whenever a problem came up on the site drawings, he walked to Sudha ma'am's desk. "Ma'am, what should I do?" In three months he had asked her about beam sizes, email wording, and once, where to eat lunch.
On Thursday she didn't look up from her screen. "Uday, before you ask me anything today, bring me two options and which one you'd choose."
He went back to his desk, irritated, and stared at the drainage problem. Slowly he sketched one fix, then another. The second was cheaper but meant rerouting a pipe. He wrote down why he'd pick it.
At four he returned. "Option A, option B. I'd go with B because..."
She listened, asked one question he hadn't thought of, and nodded. "Good. Adjust for that and send it."
Walking back, he felt taller than he had in weeks. The next morning he solved a smaller problem without going to her at all.

qa.q: What had Uday asked Sudha ma'am about in three months?
qa.a: Beam sizes, email wording, and once, where to eat lunch.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when Sudha ma'am asked for two options?
qa.a: Irritated at first, then, after presenting his own choice, proud and taller than he had felt in weeks.

qa.q: What habit did Sudha ma'am's request build?
qa.a: Bringing his own options and a recommendation, which grew his judgement until he solved the next problem alone.

qa.q: Why might Sudha ma'am have stopped answering directly?
qa.a: She could see him handing her every decision and wanted him to build independent judgement.

grounding: Shows waiting for a mentor to decide everything, and growing into independent judgement by bringing one's own ideas.

passage:
Dear Dr. Sarita,
For the last six months I've come to every meeting asking you what I should do next, and you've always answered patiently. I realised last week that I've never once come with my own plan. That isn't fair to you, and it isn't helping me grow as a researcher.
So this time I'm sending an idea first. For the next chapter, I'd like to compare the flood records from the two districts using the rainfall data I cleaned in April. I've written a one-page outline with two possible methods. I lean towards the second because it handles the missing years better, but I'm unsure about the sample size.
Could we discuss this on Monday? I'd value your view on the weak points. And if you think it's the wrong direction, I'd like to understand why, so I can judge better next time.
Thank you for your patience with me.
Bhupen

qa.q: When did Bhupen clean the rainfall data?
What did Bhupen realise last week, and how does it seem to feel?
qa.a: That every meeting had been spent asking what to do; Bhupen feels a little embarrassed and determined to grow as a researcher.

qa.q: How does Bhupen's email move from dependence towards independence?
qa.a: It brings a proposed chapter, a one-page outline with two methods and a reasoned preference, and asks for critique rather than instructions.

qa.q: How might Dr. Sarita read this email?
qa.a: Pleased and encouraged to see Bhupen thinking independently, and ready to discuss the weak points on Monday.

grounding: Illustrates relying on a mentor for every decision and choosing to bring one's own ideas to build independent judgement.
